references.text: The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 26:75|Matthew 26:75] describes the same moment when Peter went out and wept bitterly after denying Jesus three times, just as Jesus had predicted.
[ref:Mark 14:72|Mark 14:72] is the parallel account where Peter breaks down in tears after remembering Jesus' words that he would deny him three times before the rooster crowed twice.

In [ref:Luk 22:34|Luke 22:34], Jesus predicts that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows. Peter's bitter weeping in verse 62 is the direct fulfillment of this prediction and an expression of his deep remorse.

[ref:Luk 22:54-61|Luke 22:54–61] provides the full context for Peter's denial. Three times Peter denies knowing Jesus, and when the rooster crows, the Lord turns and looks at Peter—leading to his bitter weeping in verse 62.
In [ref:Sal 6:7|Psalm 6:7], David describes how he drenches his bed with tears of sorrow and repentance. Peter's bitter weeping reflects these deep tears of remorse also found in the Psalms.

[ref:Sal 51:3-6|Psalm 51:3–6] is David's great penitential psalm where he confesses his sin and asks for mercy. Peter's bitter weeping expresses the same deep sorrow over having failed, pointing toward the path of repentance.

[ref:2 Kor 7:10|2 Corinthians 7:10] distinguishes between godly grief that leads to repentance and salvation, and worldly grief that leads to death. Peter's bitter weeping is an example of a godly sorrow that leads to true repentance.

[ref:Joh 21:15-17|John 21:15–17] tells of Peter's restoration after the resurrection, where Jesus asks three times if Peter loves him—corresponding to the three denials. Peter's bitter weeping in Luke 22:62 was the beginning of a process of repentance that is completed here.
